title: On-chip quantum sensing of Kondo spins in a high-mobility quasi-one-dimensional nanoconstriction
authors: Shun-Tsung Lo, Che-Cheng Wang, Sheng-Chin Ho, Jun-Hao Chang, Ming-Wei Chen, G. L. Creeth, L. W. Smith, Shih-Hsiang Chao, Yu-Chiang Hsieh, Pei-Tzu Wu, Yi-Cheng Wu, Chi-Te Liang, M. Pepper, J. P. Griffiths, I. Farrer, G. A. C. Jones, D. A. Ritchie, Tse-Ming Chen
abstract: The precise nature of Kondo spins has remained enigmatic when extended to multiple spin impurities or, more intriguingly, when the localized spin itself may already be the consequence of many-body interactions in a presumably-delocalized open nanoconstriction, such as a quantum point contact (QPC). It is experimentally challenging to distinguish the Kondo state from other coexisting many-body spin states in such a strongly correlated system. Here we lithographically define an all-on-chip electronic resonator (ER) and a QPC in a high-mobility GaAs/AlGaAs heterostructure transistor. Local Kondo screening of the QPC spin and nonlocal spin singlet across the ER-QPC integration are controllable in response to ER occupancy parity. We also show that the 0.7 anomaly, another strongly-correlated state in QPCs, not only has a different physical origin but furthermore counteracts the Kondo spin singlet. These results demonstrate a noninvasive quantum method for sensing spontaneous magnetic impurities within an open nanoconstriction.
summary: The researchers engineered a novel on-chip device combining a Quantum Point Contact with an electronic resonator to study Kondo spins. By controlling the ER's spin parity, they achieved noninvasive detection of two-impurity Kondo effects via characteristic double-peak Zero-Bias Anomalies. This work clarifies that the Kondo physics is distinct from the origin of the anomalous 0.7 conductance plateau.
main_problem: The primary challenge is experimentally distinguishing the Kondo screening state from other complex, coexisting many-body spin states within strongly correlated quasi-one-dimensional nanoconstrictions like Quantum Point Contacts (QPCs).
main_result: The authors demonstrated a noninvasive quantum sensing method by using an integrated electronic resonator (ER) to controllably induce and detect two-impurity Kondo effects, while also showing that the 0.7 anomaly counteracts these fluctuations.
method: They utilized lithographically defined all-on-chip devices combining a QPC with an ER in a high-mobility GaAs/AlGaAs heterostructure, measuring linear and nonlinear conductance (Zero-Bias Anomalies) as a function of gate voltages.
model_or_system: The system involves coupling the localized spin moment within a QPC to a tunable spin state residing in an adjacent electronic resonator (ER). This setup allows for the study of two-impurity Kondo physics and its competition with the anomalous 0.7 conductance plateau.
key_observables: Zero-Bias Anomaly (ZBA) peaks, which change from single-peak to double-peak depending on the ER occupancy parity; linear conductance oscillations related to ER filling; and the magnitude of the $0.7$ anomaly.
important_parameters: Temperature ($T$), magnetic field ($B$), gate voltages controlling QPC/ER occupancy, and the ratio of coupling strengths between impurities.
main_assumptions: The study assumes that the observed ZBA features are robust indicators of Kondo screening, despite the presence of other strong correlation effects like the 0.7 anomaly.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the device structure (QPC + ER), show characteristic linear and nonlinear conductance maps, detail how alternating single/double-peak ZBAs correlate with ER filling parity, and demonstrate the suppression of these features upon increasing temperature or magnetic field.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical platform (ER-QPC) to address the ambiguity in spin state identification. It then systematically measures transport properties, using the change in ZBA structure (single vs. double peak) as a diagnostic tool to prove nonlocal control over Kondo screening and differentiate it from the physics causing the 0.7 anomaly.
why_interesting: This work provides an exquisite experimental platform for probing fundamental many-body quantum phenomena—specifically, the competition between different types of spin correlations (Kondo vs. $0.7$ anomaly) in nanoscale conductors—which is highly relevant to understanding correlated electron physics in mesoscopic systems.
